questions.question: The chapter's epigraph is from which author and work?

options.text: John Gall, Systemantics (1975)
Donald Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming (1968)
Doug McIlroy, the Unix philosophy (1978)
Pat Helland, Immutability Changes Everything (2015)

questions.explanation: Gall's law warns that complex systems must be grown from simple working ones — which is what the chapter does: a log is an append-only file, and a stream broker is built from it.

questions.question: What was the one big assumption throughout Chapter 10, and why is it load-bearing?

options.text: That the input is bounded — of a known and finite size — so the batch process knows when it has finished reading its input. Bounded input is what makes completion meaningful
That the input fits in memory on one machine
That the input is sorted by key
That the input is immutable

questions.explanation: Chapter 10 read a set of files as input and produced a new set of output files — derived data, meaning a dataset that can be recreated by running the batch process again if necessary, as with search indexes, recommendation systems and analytics.

questions.question: Why does the chapter say a real dataset is never complete?

options.text: Because in reality a lot of data is unbounded: it arrives gradually over time, as users produce data today and tomorrow and forever. So batch processors must artificially divide the data into chunks of fixed duration
Because datasets are always too large to read fully
Because databases delete old data automatically
Because data is always corrupted at the edges

questions.explanation: Artificial chunking is what batch processing does to an unbounded reality.

questions.question: Trace the argument from daily batch to stream processing.

options.text: The problem with daily batch processes is that changes in the input are only reflected in the output a day later, which is too slow for many impatient users. To reduce the delay we can run the processing more frequently — say, processing a second's worth of data at the end of every second — or even continuously, abandoning the fixed time slices entirely and simply processing every event as it happens. That is the idea behind stream processing
Daily batch becomes hourly, then minutely, and stops there
Batch is replaced by request/response processing
Batch is replaced by in-memory databases

questions.explanation: Abandoning fixed time slices entirely is the endpoint of the argument.

questions.question: Give the general definition of 'stream' and where it already appears. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: In general a stream refers to data that is incrementally made available over time
It appears in the stdin and stdout of Unix, and in programming languages as lazy lists
It appears in filesystem APIs such as Java's FileInputStream, and in TCP connections
It appears in delivering audio and video over the internet

questions.explanation: The chapter narrows it to event streams as a data management mechanism — the unbounded, incrementally processed counterpart to the batch data of the last chapter.

questions.question: Give the chapter's definition of an event.

options.text: A small, self-contained, immutable object containing the details of something that happened at some point in time. An event usually contains a timestamp indicating when it happened according to a time-of-day clock
A mutable record that is updated as circumstances change
A batch of records grouped by time window
A message acknowledgment sent by a consumer

questions.explanation: The thing that happened might be an action a user took, such as viewing a page or making a purchase, or it may originate from a machine — such as a periodic measurement from a temperature sensor, or a CPU utilization metric. In the batch-with-Unix-tools example, each line of the web server log is an event.

questions.question: Once an event is encoded, what does that enable?

options.text: Storage — you can store an event, for example by appending it to a file, inserting it into a relational table, or writing it to a document database. And transmission — it also allows you to send the event over the network to another node in order to process it
Only storage; transmission requires a different encoding
Only transmission; events are never stored
Neither; encoding is purely for compression

questions.explanation: One encoding serves both persistence and the wire.

questions.question: Give the vocabulary for stream participants and the streaming analogue of a filename.

options.text: An event is generated once by a producer — also known as a publisher or sender — and then potentially processed by multiple consumers, also called subscribers or recipients. In a filesystem, a filename identifies a set of related records; in a streaming system, related events are usually grouped together into a topic or stream
A writer and readers; the analogue is a partition
A leader and followers; the analogue is a log segment
A coordinator and participants; the analogue is a directory

questions.explanation: Analogous to how a file is written once and then potentially read by multiple jobs.

questions.question: Why does the chapter reject using a plain file or database to connect producers and consumers?

options.text: In principle it is sufficient: a producer writes every event it generates to the datastore, and each consumer periodically polls the datastore to check for events that have appeared since it last ran — which is essentially what a batch process does when it processes a day's worth of data at the end of every day. But when moving toward continuous processing with low delays, polling becomes expensive if the datastore is not designed for this kind of usage: the more often you poll, the lower the percentage of requests that return new events, and thus the higher the overheads become. Instead it is better for consumers to be notified when new events appear
Because databases cannot store events
Because files cannot be appended to
Because polling is impossible over a network

questions.explanation: Databases do have triggers, which can react to a change such as a row being inserted into a table, but they are very limited in what they can do and have somewhat been an afterthought in database design — so specialized tools have been developed for delivering event notifications.

questions.question: Define a messaging system and what it adds over a Unix pipe or TCP connection.

options.text: A producer sends a message containing the event, which is then pushed to consumers. A Unix pipe or TCP connection between producer and consumer would be a simple way of implementing a messaging system, but most messaging systems expand on this basic model: notably, a Unix pipe or TCP connection connects exactly one sender with one recipient, whereas a messaging system allows multiple producer nodes to send messages to the same topic and allows multiple consumer nodes to receive messages in a topic
It adds only durability, not multiplicity
It adds only ordering, not multiplicity
It adds nothing; a pipe is equivalent

questions.explanation: Many-to-many rather than one-to-one is the structural addition.

questions.question: Which two questions does the chapter say are particularly helpful for distinguishing messaging systems? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: What happens if the producers send messages faster than the consumers can process them?
What happens if nodes crash or temporarily go offline — are any messages lost?
What query language does the system support?
How many partitions can a topic have?

questions.explanation: Within the publish/subscribe model there is no one right answer for all purposes, so these two questions differentiate the systems.

questions.question: Name the three broad options when producers outrun consumers.

options.text: Drop messages, buffer messages in a queue, or apply backpressure — also known as flow control, which means blocking the producer from sending more messages. Unix pipes and TCP use backpressure: they have a small fixed-size buffer, and if it fills up, the sender is blocked until the recipient takes data out of the buffer
Drop, retry, or abort
Buffer, compress, or partition
Replicate, shard, or cache

questions.explanation: If messages are buffered in a queue it is important to understand what happens as that queue grows: does the system crash if the queue no longer fits in memory, or does it write messages to disk — and if so, how does the disk access affect the performance of the messaging system?

questions.question: What does durability cost, and what do you buy by giving it up?

options.text: As with databases, durability may require some combination of writing to disk and/or replication, which has a cost. If you can afford to sometimes lose messages, you can probably get higher throughput and lower latency on the same hardware
Durability is free; giving it up buys nothing
Durability costs storage only, and buys no performance back
Durability costs latency, and giving it up reduces throughput

questions.explanation: Whether message loss is acceptable depends very much on the application: with sensor readings and metrics transmitted periodically, an occasional missing data point is perhaps not important since an updated value will be sent after a short time anyway — but beware that if a large number of messages are dropped, it may not be immediately apparent that the metrics are incorrect. If you are counting events, it is more important that they are delivered reliably, since every lost message means incorrect counters.

questions.question: What strong reliability guarantee does the chapter credit to batch systems?

options.text: That failed tasks are automatically retried and partial output from failed tasks is automatically discarded — so the output is the same as if no failure had occurred, which helps simplify the programming model
That no task ever fails
That output is written before input is read
That all output is replicated three times

questions.explanation: This is the bar the chapter sets for stream processing, which becomes the exactly-once discussion later.

questions.question: Which direct-messaging approaches does the chapter list that work without an intermediary node? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: UDP multicast, widely used in the financial industry for streams such as stock market feeds where low latency is important — although UDP itself is unreliable, application-level protocols can recover lost packets, with the producer remembering packets it has sent so it can retransmit them on demand
Brokerless messaging libraries such as ZeroMQ and nanomsg, which implement publish/subscribe messaging over TCP or IP multicast

StatsD and Brubeck use unreliable UDP messaging for collecting metrics from all machines on the network and monitoring them — note that in the StatsD protocol, counter metrics are only correct if all messages are received, making UDP counters at best approximate
Direct HTTP or RPC requests, as with webhooks, a pattern in which a callback URL of one service is registered with another service, making a request to that URL whenever an event occurs

questions.explanation: Although these direct messaging systems work well in the situations for which they are designed, they generally require the application code to be aware of the possibility of message loss: the faults they can tolerate are quite limited, since they assume that producers and consumers are constantly online. If a consumer is offline it may miss messages that were sent while it was unreachable, and although some protocols allow the producer to retry failed deliveries, that approach may break down if the producer crashes, losing the buffer of messages that it was supposed to retry.

questions.question: Define a message broker and what centralizing data in it buys.

options.text: A message broker, also known as a message queue, is essentially a kind of database that is optimized for handling message streams. It runs as a server, with producers and consumers connecting to it as clients: producers write messages to the broker and consumers receive them by reading them from the broker. By centralizing the data in the broker, these systems can more easily tolerate clients that come and go — connect, disconnect and crash — and the question of durability is moved to the broker instead. Some brokers only keep messages in memory while others write them to disk so they are not lost in case of a broker crash. Faced with slow consumers, they generally allow unbounded queueing, as opposed to dropping messages or backpressure
A broker is a stateless router with no storage
A broker is a client library, not a server
A broker always applies backpressure rather than queueing

questions.explanation: A consequence of queueing is that consumers are generally asynchronous: when a producer sends a message it normally only waits for the broker to confirm that it has buffered the message, and does not wait for the message to be processed by consumers. The delivery to consumers will happen at some undetermined future point in time — often within a fraction of a second, but sometimes significantly later if there is a queue backlog.

questions.question: Which differences between message brokers and databases does the chapter list? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Retention: databases usually keep data until it is explicitly deleted, whereas most message brokers automatically delete a message when it has been successfully delivered to its consumers — so they are not suitable for long-term data storage

Working set: since brokers quickly delete messages, most of them assume their working set is fairly small, so if the broker needs to buffer a lot of messages — perhaps spilling to disk if they no longer fit in memory — each individual message takes longer to process and overall throughput may degrade

Selection mechanism: databases often support secondary indexes and various ways of searching for data, while brokers often support some way of subscribing to a subset of topics matching some pattern — the mechanisms are different, but both are essentially ways for a client to select the portion of the data that it wants to know about

Staleness and notification: querying a database is typically based on a point-in-time snapshot of the data — if another client subsequently writes something, the first client does not find out that its result is now outdated unless it repeats or polls the query. By contrast, message brokers do not support arbitrary queries, but they do notify clients when data changes

questions.explanation: Four differences. This traditional view of message brokers is encapsulated in the JMS and AMQP standards, implemented in RabbitMQ, ActiveMQ, HornetQ, Qpid, TIBCO Enterprise Message Service, IBM MQ, Azure Service Bus and Google Cloud Pub/Sub — and some brokers can even participate in two-phase commit protocols using XA or JTA, making them quite similar in nature to databases.

questions.question: Define the two patterns for multiple consumers on a topic, and their standard names.

options.text: Load balancing: each message is delivered to one of the consumers, so the consumers can share the work of processing the messages in the topic — the broker may assign messages to consumers arbitrarily, which is useful when the messages are expensive to process so you want to add consumers to parallelize the processing. In AMQP you can implement load balancing by having multiple clients consuming from the same queue, and in JMS it is called a shared subscription. Fan-out: each message is delivered to all of the consumers, allowing several independent consumers to each 'tune in' to the same broadcast of messages without affecting each other — the streaming equivalent of having several different batch jobs that read the same input file. This is provided by topic subscriptions in JMS and exchange bindings in AMQP
Load balancing delivers to all consumers; fan-out delivers to one
Both deliver to all consumers, differing only in ordering
Both deliver to one consumer, differing only in selection

questions.explanation: The two patterns can be combined: for example, two separate groups of consumers may each subscribe to a topic such that each group collectively receives all messages, but within each group only one of the nodes receives each message.

questions.question: Why do brokers need acknowledgments, and what problem does redelivery introduce?

options.text: In order to ensure that a message is not lost, brokers use acknowledgments: a client must explicitly tell the broker when it has finished processing a message so the broker can remove it from the queue. If the connection to a client is closed or times out without the broker receiving an acknowledgment, it assumes the message was not processed and delivers the message again to another consumer. It could happen that the message actually was fully processed but the acknowledgment was lost in the network, and handling that case requires an atomic commit protocol
Acknowledgments are only for flow control; redelivery is impossible
Acknowledgments prevent reordering; redelivery causes loss
Acknowledgments are optional and introduce no problems

questions.explanation: A lost acknowledgment on a successfully processed message is exactly the exactly-once problem in miniature.

questions.question: Consumers 1 and 2 share a topic by load balancing. Consumer 2 crashes while processing m3 while consumer 1 is on m4. What order does consumer 1 see?

options.text: Consumer 1 processes m4, then m3, then m5 — because m3 is redelivered to it after consumer 2 crashes. So m3 and m4 are not delivered in the same order as they were sent by producer 1
Consumer 1 processes m3, m4, m5 in order
m3 is lost and consumer 1 processes m4, m5
Consumer 1 processes m5, m4, m3

questions.explanation: Even though the broker otherwise tries to preserve the order of messages — as required by both the JMS and AMQP standards — the combination of load balancing with redelivery inevitably leads to messages being reordered. To avoid this you can use a separate queue per consumer, that is, not use the load balancing feature. Message reordering is not a problem if messages are completely independent of each other, but it can be important if there are causal dependencies between messages.

questions.question: Contrast the transient messaging mindset with the database mindset, and its effect on derived data.

options.text: Sending a packet over a network or making a request to a network service is normally a transient operation that leaves no permanent trace, whereas everything written to a database or file is normally expected to be permanently recorded. AMQP/JMS-style brokers quickly delete messages after they have been delivered to consumers, because they are built around a transient messaging mindset. The impact on derived data: with batch processes you can repeatedly run the same process on the same input files and get the same result, but this is not the case with AMQP/JMS-style messaging — receiving a message is destructive if the acknowledgment causes it to be deleted from the broker, so you cannot run the same consumer again and expect to get the same result
Both mindsets are permanent; the difference is only in latency
Both mindsets are transient; databases also delete on read
The messaging mindset is permanent and the database mindset transient

questions.explanation: If you add a new consumer to a messaging system, it typically only starts receiving messages sent after the time it was registered; any prior messages are already gone and cannot be recovered. Contrast this with files and databases, where you can add a new client at any time and it can read data written arbitrarily far in the past.

questions.question: What question motivates log-based message brokers?

options.text: Why can we not have a hybrid, combining the durable storage approach of databases with the low-latency notification facilities of messaging? This is the idea behind log-based message brokers
Why can we not eliminate brokers entirely?
Why can we not make messaging synchronous?
Why can we not store messages in a relational table?

questions.explanation: Database durability plus messaging notification is the hybrid.

questions.question: Define a log, and describe how it works as a broker.

options.text: A log is simply an append-only sequence of records on disk — the book has used logs in the context of log-structured storage engines and write-ahead logs in Chapter 3, and in the context of replication in Chapter 5. The same structure can implement a message broker: a producer sends a message by appending it to the end of the log, and a consumer receives messages by reading the log sequentially. If a consumer reaches the end of the log, it waits for a notification that a new message has been appended — the Unix tool tail -f, which watches a file for data being appended, essentially works like this
A log is a searchable index; producers insert and consumers query
A log is a mutable file; producers overwrite the head
A log is an in-memory buffer; producers and consumers share it

questions.explanation: In order to scale to higher throughput than a single disk can offer, the log can be partitioned, with each partition a separate log that can be read and written independently of other partitions — and a topic can then be defined as a group of partitions that all carry messages of the same type.

questions.question: What does the broker assign within each partition, and what ordering guarantee results?

options.text: Within each partition the broker assigns a monotonically increasing sequence number, or offset, to every message. That makes sense because a partition is append-only, so the messages within a partition are totally ordered — but there is no ordering guarantee across different partitions
A global sequence number, giving a total order across the topic
A timestamp, giving order by event time
A hash, giving no ordering

questions.explanation: Per-partition total order, no cross-partition order. Apache Kafka, Amazon Kinesis Streams and Twitter's DistributedLog are log-based message brokers that work like this; Google Cloud Pub/Sub is architecturally similar but exposes a JMS-style API rather than a log abstraction. These brokers can deliver millions of messages per second by partitioning across multiple machines, and achieve fault tolerance by replicating messages.

questions.question: How does a log broker get fan-out and load balancing?

options.text: Fan-out comes for free, because several consumers can independently read the log without affecting each other — reading a message does not delete it from the log. To achieve load balancing across a group of consumers, instead of assigning individual messages to consumer clients the broker can assign entire partitions to nodes in the consumer group: each client then consumes all the messages in the partitions it has been assigned, typically reading them sequentially in a straightforward single-threaded manner
Both require deleting messages after delivery
Fan-out requires duplicating the log; load balancing assigns individual messages
Neither is possible with a log

questions.explanation: This coarse-grained load balancing has downsides: the number of nodes sharing the work of consuming a topic can be at most the number of log partitions in that topic, because messages within the same partition are delivered to the same node. And if a single message is slow to process, it holds up the processing of subsequent messages in that partition — a form of head-of-line blocking. A footnote offers workarounds: two consumers could share a partition by each reading a fraction of the messages, for example one reading even-numbered offsets and the other odd-numbered; or you could spread message processing over a thread pool, but that complicates consumer offset management. In general, single-threaded processing of a partition is preferable, and parallelism can be increased by using more partitions.

questions.question: Which broker style suits which workload?

options.text: In situations where messages may be expensive to process and you want to parallelize processing on a message-by-message basis, and where message ordering is not so important, the JMS/AMQP style of message broker is preferable. On the other hand, in situations with high message throughput where each message is fast to process and message ordering is important, the log-based approach works very well
Log-based suits expensive messages; JMS/AMQP suits high throughput
Both suit all workloads equally
JMS/AMQP suits ordered workloads; log-based suits unordered ones

questions.explanation: Per-message parallelism versus throughput with ordering.

questions.question: Why can a log broker stop tracking per-message acknowledgments?

options.text: Because in a partition messages are read sequentially, so all messages with an offset less than a consumer's current offset have already been processed and all messages with a greater offset have not yet been seen. Thus the broker does not need to track acknowledgments for every single message — it only needs to periodically record the consumer offsets. The reduced bookkeeping overhead and the opportunities for batching and pipelining in this approach help increase the throughput of log-based systems
Because messages are never lost, so acknowledgments are unnecessary
Because consumers acknowledge in batches of 1,000
Because the broker deletes messages on read

questions.explanation: The consumer offset is in fact very similar to the log sequence number commonly found in single-leader database replication: the broker behaves like a leader database and the consumer like a follower, and the sequence number lets a disconnected follower reconnect and resume without skipping writes.

questions.question: A consumer node in a group dies. What happens, and where do duplicates come from?

options.text: Another node in the consumer group is assigned the failed consumer's partitions, and it starts consuming messages at the last recorded offset. If the failed consumer had processed subsequent messages but not yet recorded their offset, those messages will be processed a second time upon restart
The partition is left unassigned until the node returns
The messages are lost permanently
The whole consumer group restarts from offset 0

questions.explanation: The gap between processing and offset recording is the duplicate window.

questions.question: How does a log broker avoid running out of disk?

options.text: The log is divided into segments, and from time to time old segments are deleted or moved to archive storage. So if a slow consumer cannot keep up with the rate of messages, and it falls so far behind that its consumer offset points to a deleted segment, it will miss some of the messages. Effectively the log implements a bounded-size buffer that discards old messages when it gets full — also known as a circular buffer or ring buffer — but since that buffer is on disk, it can be quite large
Messages are deleted after acknowledgment, as with JMS brokers
Messages are compressed indefinitely and never deleted
The broker refuses writes when the disk fills

questions.explanation: A disk-backed ring buffer rather than a delete-on-ack queue.

questions.question: Using a 6 TB drive with 150 MB/s sequential write throughput, how long does it take to fill the disk, and what conclusions follow?

options.text: About 11 hours — so the disk can buffer 11 hours' worth of messages. This ratio remains the same even if you use many hard drives and machines, so adding hardware buys throughput, not buffer time. In practice deployments rarely use the full write bandwidth of the disk, so the log can typically keep a buffer of several days' or even weeks' worth of messages
About 11 minutes, so buffering is negligible
About 11 days, growing with the number of machines
About 1 hour, and the ratio improves with more disks

questions.explanation: 6 TB divided by 150 MB/s is 40,000 seconds, which is about 11 hours. Regardless of how long you retain messages, the throughput of a log remains more or less constant since every message is written to disk anyway — behaviour that contrasts with messaging systems that keep messages in memory by default and only write to disk if the queue grows too large, which are fast when queues are short and become much slower when they start writing to disk, so throughput depends on the amount of history retained.

questions.question: Where does the log-based approach sit in the drop/buffer/backpressure taxonomy?

options.text: It is a form of buffering with a large but fixed-size buffer, limited by the available disk space — and it effectively drops old messages for consumers that fall too far behind
It applies backpressure to producers
It drops new messages when full
It is outside the taxonomy

questions.explanation: Buffer first, drop the oldest only when the buffer wraps.

questions.question: Which operational advantages does the chapter claim from the log's large buffer? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Time to react: you can monitor how far a consumer is behind the head of the log and raise an alert if it falls behind significantly — and because the buffer is large, there is enough time for a human operator to fix the slow consumer and let it catch up before it starts missing messages
Isolation: if a consumer does fall too far behind and begins missing messages, only that consumer is affected; it does not disrupt the service for other consumers
Safe experimentation: you can experimentally consume a production log for development, testing or debugging purposes, without having to worry much about disrupting production services

Cheap shutdown: when a consumer is shut down or crashes, it stops consuming resources — the only thing that remains is its consumer offset. This is a big contrast to traditional message brokers, where you need to be careful to delete any queues whose consumers have been shut down, otherwise they continue unnecessarily accumulating messages and taking away memory from consumers that are still active

questions.explanation: Four advantages, all consequences of read-only, non-destructive consumption.

questions.question: How do offsets make replay possible, and what does that make log-based messaging resemble?

options.text: In a log-based message broker, consuming messages is more like reading from a file: it is a read-only operation that does not change the log. The only side effect of processing, besides any output of the consumer, is that the consumer offset moves forward — but the offset is under the consumer's control, so you can easily manipulate it if necessary. For example you can start a copy of a consumer with yesterday's offsets and write the output to a different location, in order to reprocess the last day's worth of messages, and repeat this any number of times, varying the processing code. This aspect makes log-based messaging more like the batch processes of the last chapter, where derived data is clearly separated from input data through a repeatable transformation process — and it allows more experimentation and easier recovery from errors and bugs, making it a good tool for integrating dataflows within an organization
Replay requires re-sending messages from the producer
Replay is impossible once offsets advance
Replay resembles request/response processing

questions.explanation: Offsets under consumer control are what make a stream reprocessable like a file.

questions.question: What observation opens the door to applying stream ideas to databases?

options.text: The fact that a replication log is basically a stream of database write events, produced by the leader as it processes transactions — the follower applies that stream of writes to its own copy of the database, and thus ends up with an accurate copy of the same data. The events in the replication log describe the data changes that occurred. The connection between logs and databases is deeper than just the physical storage of logs on disk — it is quite fundamental
That databases can be used as message brokers
That streams can be stored in tables
That both use disks

questions.explanation: State machine replication: if every event represents a write to the database, and every replica processes the same events in the same order, then the replicas will all end up in the same final state — processing an event being assumed to be a deterministic operation.

questions.question: Why does a nontrivial application end up with several data systems, and what obligation follows?

options.text: Because there is no single system that can satisfy all data storage, querying and processing needs: in practice most nontrivial applications need to combine several different technologies — an OLTP database to serve user requests, a cache to speed up common requests, a full-text index to handle search queries, and a data warehouse for analytics. Each of these has its own copy of the data, stored in its own representation optimized for its own purposes, and since the same or related data appears in several places, they need to be kept in sync with one another
Because databases are unreliable, so redundancy is needed
Because different teams prefer different products
Because a single system would be too expensive

questions.explanation: With data warehouses this synchronization is usually performed by ETL processes, often by taking a full copy of a database, transforming it, and bulk-loading it into the data warehouse — in other words a batch process. Search indexes, recommendation systems and other derived data systems might be created the same way.

questions.question: Define dual writes, and trace the race in Figure 11-4.

options.text: Dual writes means the application code explicitly writes to each of the systems when data changes — for example first writing to the database, then updating the search index, then invalidating the cache entries, or even performing those writes concurrently. In the race, two clients concurrently set item X: client 1 sets it to A and client 2 to B. Both write to the database, and the requests interleave unluckily — the database sees client 1's write (A) then client 2's write (B), ending at B, while the search index sees client 2's write (B) then client 1's write (A), ending at A. The two systems are now permanently inconsistent with each other, even though no error occurred
Dual writes means writing twice to the same system; the race causes duplicate rows
Dual writes means replicating to two replicas; the race causes lost writes
Dual writes means writing synchronously to both; no race is possible

questions.explanation: Unless you have some additional concurrency detection mechanism such as version vectors, you will not even notice that concurrent writes occurred — one value will simply silently overwrite another.

questions.question: What is the second problem with dual writes, and the chapter's diagnosis?

options.text: That one of the writes may fail while the other succeeds — for example the database write succeeds but the search index update fails — which is a fault-tolerance problem rather than a concurrency problem, and which is the atomic commit problem, expensive to solve. The diagnosis: if you only have one replicated database with a single leader, that leader determines the order of writes, so state machine replication works among replicas of the database. However, in Figure 11-4 there isn't a single leader — the database may have a leader and the search index may have a leader, but neither follows the other, so conflicts can occur. The situation would be better if there really was only one leader — for example the database — and if we could make the search index a follower of the database. But is this possible in practice?
That the writes are too slow; the diagnosis is network latency
That the writes use different formats; the diagnosis is encoding
That the writes are unordered; the diagnosis is clock skew

questions.explanation: Two independent leaders with no ordering relationship is the root cause.

questions.question: Why was making the search index a follower historically hard, and what is the name for doing it anyway?

options.text: Because the replication log has long been considered an internal implementation detail of the database, not a public API — clients are supposed to query the database through its data model and query language, not parse the replication logs and attempt to extract data from them. For decades many databases simply did not have a documented way of getting the log of changes written to them. The name for doing it anyway is change data capture (CDC): the process of observing all data changes written to a database and extracting them in a form in which they can be replicated to other systems, and it is especially interesting if changes are made available as a stream, immediately as they are written
Because search indexes cannot accept replication logs; the name is ETL
Because databases forbid it contractually; the name is log shipping
Because replication logs are encrypted; the name is event sourcing

questions.explanation: An undocumented internal log is what made CDC a reverse-engineering exercise.

questions.question: What does CDC do to the topology of your systems, and why is a log-based broker the right transport?

options.text: Change data capture makes one database the leader — the one from which the changes are captured — and turns the others into followers. A log-based message broker is well suited for transporting the change events from the source database, since it preserves the ordering of messages, avoiding the reordering issue seen with load-balancing brokers
It makes all systems peers; a JMS broker is the right transport
It makes the search index the leader; any broker will do
It removes leaders entirely; no broker is needed

questions.explanation: Taking data in the order it was written to one database and applying the changes to other systems in the same order means the data in the search index will match the data in the database — and the data stored in the search index and the data warehouse is just another view onto the data in the system of record.

questions.question: Compare the two implementation techniques for CDC.

options.text: Database triggers can be used to implement change data capture by registering triggers that observe all changes to data tables and add corresponding entries to a changelog table — but they tend to be fragile and have significant performance overheads. Parsing the replication log can be a more robust approach, although it also comes with challenges, such as handling schema changes
Triggers are robust; log parsing is fragile
Both are equally robust with no performance difference
Only triggers are possible; replication logs cannot be parsed

questions.explanation: LinkedIn's Databus, Facebook's Wormhole and Yahoo!'s Sherpa use this idea at large scale.

questions.question: Match each CDC tool to its source database and mechanism.

options.text: Bottled Water implements CDC for PostgreSQL using an API that decodes the write-ahead log; Maxwell and Debezium do something similar for MySQL by parsing the binlog; Mongoriver reads the MongoDB oplog; and GoldenGate provides similar facilities for Oracle
Bottled Water for MySQL; Debezium for PostgreSQL; Mongoriver for Oracle
All four tools work with PostgreSQL only
All four use triggers rather than logs

questions.explanation: Change data capture is usually asynchronous: the system of record database does not wait for the change to be applied to consumers before committing it. This has the operational advantage that adding a slow consumer does not affect the system of record too much, but the downside that all the issues of replication lag apply.

questions.question: Why can't you always just replay the whole change log?

options.text: Because keeping all changes forever would require too much disk space, and replaying it would take too long — so the log needs to be truncated. For example, building a new full-text index requires a full copy of the entire database: it is not sufficient to only apply a log of recent changes, since that would still be missing items that were not recently updated. So if you don't have the entire log history you need to start with a consistent snapshot
Because the change log is encrypted
Because replaying changes them
Because the log has no ordering

questions.explanation: The snapshot of the database must correspond to a known position or offset in the change log, so that you know at which point to start applying changes after the snapshot has been processed. Some CDC tools integrate this snapshot facility, while others leave it as a manual operation.

questions.question: State the log compaction principle and the role of the tombstone.

options.text: The storage engine periodically looks for log records with the same key, throws away any duplicates, and keeps only the most recent update for each key — all in the background. In a log-structured storage engine, an update with a special null value called a tombstone indicates that a key was deleted, and causes it to be removed during log compaction. But as long as a key is not overwritten or deleted, it stays in the log forever — so the disk space required for such a compacted log depends only on the current contents of the database, not the number of writes that have ever occurred
Compaction deletes the oldest records regardless of key; tombstones mark them
Compaction merges values by summing them; tombstones are checksums
Compaction keeps the oldest update per key; tombstones mark inserts

questions.explanation: Space proportional to current contents, not to write history.

questions.question: What must the CDC system guarantee for compaction to work, and what does it let you skip?

options.text: In the context of CDC, if every change has a primary key and every update for a key replaces the previous value for that key, then it's sufficient to keep just the most recent write for a particular key. Now, whenever you want to rebuild a derived data system such as a search index, you can start a new consumer from offset 0 of the log-compacted topic and sequentially scan over all messages in the log: the log is guaranteed to contain the most recent value for every key in the database, so you can use it to get a full copy of the database contents without having to take another snapshot of the CDC source database. This feature is supported by Apache Kafka, and allows the message broker to be used for durable storage, not just for transient messaging
It must guarantee ordering only; compaction lets you skip the broker
It must guarantee at-most-once delivery; compaction lets you skip acknowledgments
It must guarantee monotonic timestamps; compaction lets you skip the log

questions.explanation: A compacted log is a snapshot, so no separate snapshot is needed.

questions.question: Which databases does the chapter credit with first-class change streams?

options.text: RethinkDB allows queries to subscribe to notifications when the results of a query change; Firebase and CouchDB provide data synchronization based on a change feed that is also made available to applications; and Meteor uses the MongoDB oplog to subscribe to data changes and update the user interface. These are first-class interfaces rather than the typical retrofitted and reverse-engineered CDC efforts
PostgreSQL, MySQL and Oracle, all with first-class change streams
Cassandra and Riak, via read repair
No database supports first-class change streams

questions.explanation: VoltDB also allows transactions to continuously export data from a database in the form of a stream: the database represents an output stream in the relational data model as a table into which transactions can insert tuples, but which cannot be queried. The stream then consists of the log of tuples that committed transactions have written to this special table, in the order they were committed, and external consumers can asynchronously consume this log.

questions.question: What is Kafka Connect, and what does it enable?

options.text: An effort to integrate change data capture tools for a wide range of database systems with Kafka. Once the stream of change events is in Kafka it can be used to update derived data systems such as search indexes, and also feed into stream processing systems
A replication protocol between Kafka clusters
A query language for Kafka topics
A partitioning scheme for Kafka

questions.explanation: CDC tooling plus a durable log gives you a general-purpose integration substrate.

questions.question: Where did event sourcing come from, and why does the chapter discuss it?

options.text: It was developed in the domain-driven design (DDD) community, and the chapter discusses it because it incorporates some useful and relevant ideas for streaming systems
It came from the Kafka community and is discussed as a Kafka feature
It came from the relational database community
It came from the functional programming community

questions.explanation: DDD origin, streaming relevance.

questions.question: State the biggest difference between CDC and event sourcing.

options.text: Event sourcing applies the idea at a different level of abstraction. In CDC the application uses the database in a mutable way, updating and deleting records at will, and the log of changes is extracted from the database at a low level — such as by parsing the replication log — which ensures that the order of writes extracted from the database matches the order in which they were actually written, avoiding the race condition of dual writes, and the application writing to the database does not need to be aware that CDC is occurring. In event sourcing the application logic is explicitly built on the basis of immutable events that are written to an event log: the event store is append-only, and updates or deletes are discouraged or prohibited, with events designed to reflect things that happened at the application level rather than low-level state changes
CDC is application-level and event sourcing is database-level
They are the same technique under two names
CDC uses immutable events and event sourcing uses mutable state

questions.explanation: Low-level state changes versus application-level facts.

questions.question: What benefits does the chapter claim for event sourcing as a data-modeling technique? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: It is more meaningful to record the user's actions as immutable events, rather than recording the effect of those actions on a mutable database
It makes it easier to evolve applications over time
It helps with debugging by making it easier to understand after the fact why something happened
It guards against application bugs

questions.explanation: In the course-enrollment example, the event 'student cancelled their course enrollment' clearly expresses the intent of a single action in a neutral fashion, whereas the side effects — one entry was deleted from the enrollments table, and one cancellation reason was added to the student feedback table — embed a lot of assumptions about the way the data is later going to be used. If a new application feature is introduced, for example 'the place is offered to the next person on the waiting list', the event sourcing approach allows that new side effect to easily be chained off the existing event.

questions.question: Which existing ideas does the chapter say event sourcing resembles, and what about tooling?

options.text: It is similar to the chronicle data model, and there are also similarities between an event log and the fact table found in a star schema. Specialized databases such as Event Store have been developed to support applications using event sourcing, but in general the approach is independent of any particular tool — a conventional database or a log-based message broker can also be used
It resembles the relational model, and requires Event Store specifically
It resembles the graph model, and requires Kafka specifically
It resembles nothing previously known, and has no tooling

questions.explanation: Chronicle data model and star-schema fact tables, with tool independence.

questions.question: Why can't you just show users the event log, and what property must the transformation have?

options.text: Users generally expect to see the current state of a system, not the history of modifications — for example on a shopping website, users expect to see the current contents of their cart, not an append-only list of all the changes they have ever made to it. So applications that use event sourcing need to take the log of events, which represents the data written to the system, and transform it into application state that is suitable for showing to a user, which is the way in which data is read from the system. This transformation can use arbitrary logic, but it should be deterministic so that you can run it again and derive the same application state from the event log
Because event logs are too large; the transformation must be lossy
Because event logs are encrypted; the transformation must decrypt
You can show the event log directly; no transformation is needed

questions.explanation: Determinism is what makes the derived state reproducible.

questions.question: Why does log compaction work for CDC but not for event sourcing?

options.text: Because with CDC, each event for an update typically contains the entire new version of the record, so the current value for a primary key is entirely determined by the most recent event for that key, and log compaction can discard previous events for the same key. Event sourcing models events at a higher level: an event typically expresses the intent of a user action, not the mechanics of the state update that occurred as a result, and in that case later events typically do not override prior events — so you need the full history of events to reconstruct the final state, and log compaction is not possible in the same way
Compaction works for both equally
Compaction works for event sourcing but not CDC
Compaction works for neither

questions.explanation: Replacement semantics versus intent semantics. Applications that use event sourcing typically do have some mechanism for storing snapshots of the current state derived from the log of events, but that is only a performance optimization to speed up reads and recovery from crashes — the intention is that the system is able to store all raw events forever and reprocess the full event log whenever required.

questions.question: Explain the distinction between commands and events, and the moment of transition.

options.text: When a request from a user first arrives it is initially a command: at this point it may still fail, for example because some integrity condition is violated. The application must first validate that it can execute the command, and if the validation is successful and the command is accepted, it becomes an event, which is durable and immutable
Commands are immutable and events are mutable
Events precede commands, which are their side effects
There is no distinction; the terms are synonyms

questions.explanation: For example, if a user tries to register a particular username, or reserve a seat on an airplane or in a theater, the application needs to check that the username or seat is not already taken. At the moment the command is accepted it becomes a fact — and if the customer later cancels a seat reservation, the fact remains true that they formerly held a reservation for that particular seat, so the change or cancellation is a separate event that is added later.

questions.question: Why must validation be synchronous, and what is the asynchronous alternative?

options.text: Because a consumer of the event stream is not allowed to reject an event: by the time the consumer sees the event it is already an immutable part of the log, and it may have already been seen by other consumers. So any validation of a command needs to happen synchronously, before it becomes an event — for example by using a serializable transaction that atomically validates the command and publishes the event. Alternatively, the user action to reserve a seat could be split into two events: first a tentative reservation, and then a separate confirmation event once the reservation has been validated — which allows the validation to take place in an asynchronous process
Validation can be asynchronous because consumers may reject events
Validation happens in the log itself
Validation is unnecessary with event sourcing

questions.explanation: Immutability forward means validation must come before the log.

questions.question: How does the chapter resolve the tension between immutable events and changing state?

options.text: Whenever you have state that changes, that state is the result of the events that mutated it over time — so however the state changes, there was always a sequence of events that caused those changes. Mutable state and an append-only log of immutable events do not contradict each other: they are two sides of the same coin. The log of all changes, the changelog, represents the evolution of state over time
State must be abandoned in favour of logs
Logs must be abandoned in favour of state
The tension is unresolvable

questions.explanation: Examples: your list of currently available seats is the result of the reservations you have processed; the current account balance is the result of the credits and debits on the account; the response time graph for your web server is an aggregation of the individual response times of all web requests that have occurred. Even as things are done and undone, the fact remains true that those events occurred.

questions.question: State the calculus analogy between state and streams.

options.text: The application state is what you get when you integrate an event stream over time, and a change stream is what you get when you differentiate the state by time. The analogy has limitations — for example the second derivative of state does not seem to be meaningful — but it's a useful starting point for thinking about data
State is the derivative of the stream and the stream is the integral of state
Both are integrals of each other
The analogy is exact with no limitations

questions.explanation: Integrate events to get state; differentiate state to get a change stream.

questions.question: Reproduce Pat Helland's formulation about logs and databases.

options.text: Transaction logs record all the changes made to the database — high-speed appends are the only way to change the log. From this perspective, the contents of the database hold a caching of the latest record values in the logs: the truth is the log, and the database is a cache of a subset of the log — namely the latest value of each record and index value from the log
The truth is the database and the log is a cache
Both are equally authoritative
Neither is authoritative; the application is

questions.explanation: Log compaction is one way of bridging the distinction between log and database state: it retains only the latest version of each record and discards overwritten versions.

questions.question: How have accountants used immutability, and what do they do about mistakes?

options.text: In finance, bookkeeping has been done with append-only ledgers for centuries — a log of events describing money, goods or services that have changed hands, from which aggregations such as profit and loss or the balance sheet are derived by adding them up. If a mistake is made, accountants don't erase or change the incorrect transaction in the ledger; instead they add another transaction that compensates for the mistake, for example refunding an incorrect charge. The incorrect transaction still remains in the ledger forever, for auditing reasons, and if the figures for the incorrect month have already been published, then the figures for the next accounting period include a correction. This process is entirely normal in accounting
Accountants erase incorrect entries and rewrite them
Accountants delete the affected period and recompute
Accountants have always used mutable ledgers

questions.explanation: Compensating transactions rather than erasure — the same discipline event sourcing adopts. Although such auditability is particularly important in financial systems, it is also beneficial for many other systems that are not subject to such strict regulation.

questions.question: A customer adds an item to their cart and then removes it. Who cares?

options.text: From the point of view of order fulfillment the two events cancel each other out, but for analytics purposes it may be useful to know that the customer was considering a particular item but then decided against it — perhaps to choose to recommend a different item, or to automatically send them a coupon. This information is recorded in an event log, but would be lost in a database that deletes items when they are removed from the cart. So immutable events also capture more information than just the current state
Nobody; the events genuinely cancel out
Only the fulfillment system cares
Only the audit system cares

questions.explanation: Immutability preserves information that mutation discards. As discussed under the philosophy of batch process outputs, recovery from buggy code is much harder if the code is able to destructively overwrite data — but with an append-only log of immutable events it is much easier to diagnose what happened and recover from the problem.

questions.question: Which systems derive read-oriented views from the same event log?

options.text: The analytic database Druid ingests directly from Kafka; Pistachio is a distributed key-value store that uses Kafka as a commit log; and Kafka Connect sinks can export data from Kafka to various different databases and indexes. It would make sense for many other storage and indexing systems, such as search servers, to similarly take their input from a distributed log
Only Kafka Streams can derive views
Only relational databases can derive views
No systems do this in practice

questions.explanation: Having an explicit translation step from an event log to a database makes it easier to evolve your application over time: if you want to introduce a new feature that presents your existing data in some new way, you can use the event log to build a separate read-optimized view for the new feature and run it alongside the existing systems without having to modify them. Running old and new systems side by side is often easier than performing a complicated schema migration in an existing system — and once the old system is no longer needed you can simply shut it down and reclaim its resources.

questions.question: Name the idea of separating write form from read form, and its effect on normalization debates.

options.text: Command query responsibility segregation (CQRS). The notion of separating the form in which data is written from the form it is read, and allowing several different read views, takes some getting used to — but it removes the fallacy that data must be written in the same form as it will be queried. Debates about normalization and denormalization become largely irrelevant if you can translate data from a write-optimized event log to read-optimized application state: it is entirely reasonable to denormalize data in the read-optimized views, since the translation process gives you a mechanism for keeping it consistent with the event log
Event sourcing; it settles the debate in favour of normalization
Materialized views; it settles the debate in favour of denormalization only for warehouses
Schema-on-read; it makes normalization mandatory

questions.explanation: Twitter's home timelines illustrate read-optimized state: a cache of recently written tweets by the people a particular user is following, like a mailbox. They are highly denormalized, since your tweets are duplicated in all of the timelines of the people following you — but the fan-out service keeps this duplicated state in sync with new tweets and new following relationships, which keeps the duplication manageable.

questions.question: What is the biggest downside of event sourcing and CDC, and what are the solutions?

options.text: That the consumers of the event log are usually asynchronous, so there is a possibility that a user may make a write to the log, then read from a log-derived view and find that their write has not yet been reflected in the read view. One solution is to perform the updates of the read view synchronously with appending the event to the log — which requires a transaction to combine the writes into an atomic unit, so you either need to keep the event log and the read view in the same storage system, or you need a distributed transaction across the different systems. Alternatively you could use the approach of implementing linearizable storage using total order broadcast
That the log grows forever; the solution is deletion
That events are mutable; the solution is checksums
That events are unordered; the solution is timestamps

questions.explanation: Reading your own writes is the specific guarantee at risk.

questions.question: How does deriving state from an event log simplify concurrency control?

options.text: Much of the need for multi-object transactions stems from a single user action requiring data to be changed in several different places. With event sourcing you can design an event such that it is a self-contained description of a user action, then the user action requires only a single write in one place — namely appending the events to the log — which is easy to make atomic. And if the event log and the application state are partitioned in the same way, for example processing an event for a customer in partition 3 only requires updating partition 3 of the application state, then a straightforward single-threaded log consumer needs no concurrency control for writes: by construction it only processes a single event at a time. The log removes the nondeterminism of concurrency by defining a serial order of events in a partition. If an event touches multiple state partitions, a bit more work is required, which Chapter 12 discusses
It requires more multi-object transactions, not fewer
It requires two-phase locking on the log
It has no effect on concurrency control

questions.explanation: A serial order per partition plus co-partitioned state removes the need for locking.

questions.question: To what extent is it feasible to keep an immutable history forever?

options.text: The answer depends on the amount of churn in the dataset. Some workloads mostly add data and rarely update or delete, and they are easy to make immutable. Other workloads have a high rate of updates and deletes on a comparatively small dataset — in these cases the immutable history may grow prohibitively large, fragmentation may become an issue, and the performance of compaction and garbage collection becomes crucial for operational robustness
Always feasible regardless of workload
Never feasible for any workload
Feasible only for read-only workloads

questions.explanation: Various databases internally use immutable data structures or multi-version data to support point-in-time snapshots, and version control systems such as Git, Mercurial and Fossil also rely on immutable data to preserve version history of files.

questions.question: What administrative reasons for deletion does the chapter give, and what do Datomic and Fossil call real deletion?

options.text: Besides the performance reasons, there may be circumstances in which you need to delete data for administrative reasons in spite of all immutability: for example privacy regulations may require deleting a user's personal information after they close their account, data protection legislation may require erroneous information to be removed, or an accidental leak of sensitive information may need to be contained. In these circumstances it's not sufficient to just append another event to the log to indicate that the prior data should be considered deleted — you actually want to rewrite history and pretend that the data was never written in the first place. Datomic calls this feature excision, and the Fossil version control system has a similar concept called shunning
Only performance reasons; the features are called compaction and vacuum
Only auditing reasons; the features are called redaction and masking
There are no administrative reasons for deletion

questions.explanation: Truly deleting data is surprisingly hard, since copies can live in many places: storage engines, filesystems and SSDs often write to a new location rather than overwriting in place, and backups are often deliberately immutable to prevent accidental deletion or corruption. Deletion is more a matter of 'making it harder to retrieve the data' than actually 'making it impossible to retrieve the data'.

questions.question: List the three broad options for what you can do with a stream. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Write it to a database, cache, search index, or similar storage system, from where it can then be queried by other clients — the streaming equivalent of keeping derived data systems up to date, and a good way of keeping a database in sync with changes happening in other parts of the system, especially if the stream consumer is the only client writing to the database

Push the events to users in some way, for example by sending email alerts or push notifications, or by streaming the events to a real-time dashboard — in this case a human is the ultimate consumer of the stream
Process one or more input streams to produce one or more output streams, which may consume streams in a pipeline consisting of several such processing stages before eventually ending up at an output
Discard the stream after computing a checksum

questions.explanation: A piece of code that processes streams like this is known as an operator or a job, closely related to the Unix processes and MapReduce jobs of Chapter 10: a stream processor consumes input streams in a read-only fashion and writes its output to a different location in an append-only fashion.

questions.question: What does the chapter say carries over from batch processing unchanged?

options.text: The patterns for partitioning and parallelization in stream processors are also very similar to those in MapReduce and the dataflow engines, and basic mapping operations such as transforming and filtering records also work the same
Sorting and sort-merge joins carry over unchanged
Fault tolerance mechanisms carry over unchanged
Nothing carries over

questions.explanation: The one crucial difference to batch jobs is that a stream never ends — which has two consequences: sorting does not make sense with an unbounded dataset, so sort-merge joins cannot be used; and fault-tolerance mechanisms must also change, since with a batch job that has been running for a few minutes a failed task can simply be restarted from the beginning, but with a stream job that has been running for several years, restarting from the beginning after a crash may not be a viable option.

questions.question: Which monitoring applications does the chapter name? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Fraud detection systems need to determine if the usage patterns of a credit card have unexpectedly changed, and block the card if it is likely to have been stolen
Trading systems need to examine price changes in a financial market and execute trades according to specified rules
Manufacturing systems need to monitor the status of machines in a factory, and quickly identify the problem if there is a malfunction
Military and intelligence systems need to track the activities of a potential aggressor, and raise the alarm if there are signs of an attack

questions.explanation: These kinds of applications require quite sophisticated pattern matching and correlations.

questions.question: When was complex event processing developed, and what is the chapter's analogy for it?

options.text: CEP is an approach developed in the 1990s for analyzing event streams, especially geared toward applications that require searching for certain event patterns. The analogy: similar to the way that you search for specific patterns of characters in a string using a regular expression, CEP allows you to specify rules to search for certain patterns of events in a stream
In the 2010s; the analogy is to SQL joins
In the 1970s; the analogy is to state machines only
In the 2000s; the analogy is to batch processing

questions.explanation: CEP systems often use a high-level declarative query language like SQL, or a graphical user interface, to describe the patterns of events that should be detected. These queries are submitted to a processing engine that consumes the input streams and internally maintains a state machine that performs the required matching, and when a match is found the engine emits a complex event — hence the name — with the details of the event pattern that was detected.

questions.question: How does CEP reverse the normal relationship between queries and data?

options.text: In these systems the relationship between queries and data is reversed compared to normal databases: usually a database stores data persistently and treats queries as transient — when a query comes in, the database searches for data matching the query, then forgets about the query when it has finished. CEP engines reverse these roles: queries are stored long-term, and events from the input streams continuously flow past them in search of a query that matches an event pattern
CEP stores data long-term and queries transiently, like a database
CEP stores neither queries nor data
CEP stores both persistently, unlike a database

questions.explanation: Persistent queries, transient data. Implementations include Esper, IBM InfoSphere Streams, Apama, TIBCO StreamBase and SQLstream, and distributed stream processors like Samza are also gaining SQL support for declarative queries on streams.

questions.question: Where does the chapter draw the boundary between CEP and stream analytics?

options.text: The boundary between CEP and stream analytics is blurry, but as a general rule, analytics tends to be less interested in finding specific event sequences and is more oriented toward aggregations and statistical metrics over a large number of events — for example measuring the rate of some type of event, calculating the rolling average of a value over some time period, or comparing current statistics to previous time intervals, such as detecting trends or alerting on metrics that are unusually high or low compared to the same time last week
The boundary is sharp: CEP is declarative and analytics is imperative
Analytics finds event sequences and CEP computes aggregates
There is no difference at all

questions.explanation: In a concrete example you might want to know the average number of queries per second to a service over the last 5 minutes, and their 99th percentile response time during that period: averaging over a few minutes smoothes out irrelevant fluctuations from one second to the next, while still giving you a timely picture of any changes in traffic pattern. The time interval over which you aggregate is known as a window.

questions.question: Which probabilistic algorithms does the chapter name, and what misconception does it correct?

options.text: Bloom filters for set membership, HyperLogLog for cardinality estimation, and various percentile estimation algorithms. Such probabilistic algorithms produce approximate results but have the advantage of requiring significantly less memory in the stream processor than exact algorithms. This use of approximation algorithms sometimes leads people to believe that stream processing systems are always lossy and inexact, but that is wrong: there is nothing inherently approximate about stream processing, and probabilistic algorithms are merely an optimization
Bloom filters only, and stream processing is indeed always approximate
HyperLogLog only, and approximation is mandatory
No probabilistic algorithms are used in streaming

questions.explanation: Many open source distributed stream processing frameworks are designed with analytics in mind — Apache Storm, Spark Streaming, Flink, Concord, Samza and Kafka Streams — and hosted services include Google Cloud Dataflow and Azure Stream Analytics.

questions.question: Why is materialized view maintenance a distinct use of stream processing?

options.text: Because deriving an alternative view onto some dataset so that you can query it efficiently, and updating that view whenever the underlying data changes, is a different kind of windowing requirement: in event sourcing the application state is also a kind of materialized view, and unlike analytics it is usually not sufficient to consider only events within some time window — building the materialized view potentially requires all events over an arbitrary time period, apart from any that may be obsolete by log compaction. In effect you need a window that stretches all the way back to the beginning of time. Samza and Kafka Streams support this kind of usage, building upon Kafka's support for log compaction
Because it requires a shorter window than analytics
Because it requires no state at all
Because it cannot be done with stream processing

questions.explanation: In principle any stream processor could be used for materialized view maintenance, although the need to maintain events forever runs counter to the assumptions of some analytics-oriented frameworks that mostly operate on windows of a limited duration.

questions.question: How does searching on streams differ from CEP and from a search engine?

options.text: Besides CEP, which allows searching for patterns consisting of multiple events, there is also sometimes a need to search for individual events based on complex criteria, such as full-text search queries. Conventional search engines first index the documents and then run queries over the index; by contrast, searching a stream turns the processing on its head: the queries are stored, and the documents run past the queries. Examples include media monitoring services that subscribe to feeds of news articles and broadcasts from media outlets and search for any news mentioning companies, products or topics of interest, and real estate websites that let users ask to be notified when a new property matching their search criteria appears on the market. The percolator feature of Elasticsearch is one option for implementing this kind of stream search — and as an optimization, it is possible to index the queries as well as the documents, narrowing down the set of queries that may match, rather than testing every document against every query
Stream search indexes documents first, like a search engine
Stream search is identical to CEP
Stream search is impossible in practice

questions.explanation: Stored queries, moving documents.

questions.question: Why don't we normally think of actor frameworks as stream processors? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Actor frameworks are primarily a mechanism for managing concurrency and distributed execution of communicating modules, whereas stream processing is primarily a data management technique
Communication between actors is often ephemeral and one-to-one, whereas event logs are durable and multi-subscriber

Actors can communicate in arbitrary ways, including cyclic request/response patterns, but stream processors are usually set up in acyclic pipelines where every stream is the output of one particular job, and derived from a well-defined set of input streams
Actors cannot process messages at all

questions.explanation: That said, there is some crossover between RPC-like systems and stream processing: Apache Storm has a feature called distributed RPC, which allows user queries to be farmed out to a set of nodes that also process event streams, with those queries interleaved with events from the input streams, and results aggregated and sent back to the user. But note that many such frameworks do not guarantee message delivery in the case of crashes, so the processing is not fault-tolerant unless you implement additional retry logic.

questions.question: Which clock does a batch process use for time breakdowns, and what does that buy it?

options.text: The timestamp embedded in each event. There is no point in looking at the system clock of the machine running the batch process, because the time at which the process is run has nothing to do with the time at which the events actually occurred — a batch process may read a year's worth of historical events within a few minutes, so in most cases the timeline of interest is the year of history, not the few minutes of processing. Moreover, using the timestamps in the events allows the processing to be deterministic: running the same process again on the same input yields the same result
The system clock of the processing machine, for determinism
The broker's clock, for consistency
A logical clock, for causality

questions.explanation: Determinism under replay is the key benefit.

questions.question: Which clock do many stream processing frameworks use for windowing, and when does it break down?

options.text: Many use the local system clock on the processing machine — the processing time — to determine windowing. This approach has the advantage of being simple, and it is reasonable if the delay between event creation and event processing is negligibly short. However it breaks down if there is any significant processing lag, that is if the processing may happen noticeably later than the time at which the event actually occurred
The event timestamp, which breaks down under clock skew
A logical clock, which breaks down at scale
The broker's ingestion time, which never breaks down

questions.explanation: Reasons for processing delay include queueing, network faults, a performance issue leading to contention in the message broker or processor, a restart of the stream consumer, or reprocessing of past events while recovering from a fault or after fixing a bug in the code.

questions.question: Two web requests are handled by servers A and B. What can the stream processor see?

options.text: Say a user first makes one web request handled by web server A, and then a second request handled by server B. Server A and server B both emit events describing the requests they handled, but B's event happens to reach the message broker before A's event does — so the stream processors will first see the B event and then the A event, even though they actually occurred in the opposite order. The general point is that message delays can also lead to unpredictable ordering of messages
The processor always sees events in the order they occurred
The processor sees only one of the two events
The processor sees both events with identical timestamps

questions.explanation: Confusing event time and processing time leads to bad data.

questions.question: Reproduce the Star Wars analogy with its years and mapping.

options.text: Star Wars movies were released in the order Episode IV in 1977, Episode V in 1980 and Episode VI in 1983, followed by Episodes I, II and III in 1999, 2002 and 2005, and Episode VII in 2015 — so the order in which the films were processed by a viewer watching them as they came out is inconsistent with the order of their narrative.
