The episode number is like the event timestamp, and the date when you watched the movie is the processing time. As humans we are able to cope with such discontinuities, but stream processing algorithms need to be specifically written to accommodate such timing and ordering issues
Episodes released I through VII in order; the analogy is about sequels
The episode number is processing time and the viewing date is event time
The analogy illustrates windowing rather than ordering

questions.explanation: A footnote thanks Kostas Kloudas from the Flink community for coming up with this analogy.

questions.question: A request-rate stream processor is redeployed and is down for a minute. What does the graph show?

options.text: If you shut down the stream consumer for a minute and process the backlog of events when it comes back up, a graph based on the processing time shows a sudden anomalous spike of requests when in fact the real rate of requests was steady. Windowing by processing time introduces artifacts due to variations in processing rate
The graph correctly shows a steady rate
The graph shows a dip during the outage and then a steady rate
The graph shows nothing at all

questions.explanation: A spike that measures the processor's recovery rather than the world's request rate.

questions.question: You are counting requests per minute in event-time windows, and events have shifted to the 38th and 39th minutes. What is the problem?

options.text: When do you declare that you have finished the window for the 37th minute and output its counter value? You can declare a window ready to close after you have not seen any new events for a while, but it could still happen that some events were buffered on another machine somewhere, delayed due to a network interruption — so you need to be able to handle such straggler events that arrive after you have declared the window complete. In general you can never be sure when you have received all of the events for a particular window, or whether there are some events still to come
The windows overlap, so events are double counted
The counter overflows
There is no problem; windows close automatically

questions.explanation: Even a timeout is not safe, because the delayed events may exceed it.

questions.question: What are the two broad options for handling straggler events?

options.text: Ignore the straggler events, since they are probably a small percentage of events in normal circumstances — though you can track the number of dropped events as a metric, and alert if you start dropping a significant amount of data. Or publish a correction, an updated value for the window with stragglers included — and you may also need to retract the previous output
Buffer indefinitely or crash
Reorder the stream or discard the window
Extend the window forever or shrink it to zero

questions.explanation: Drop with metrics, or correct with retraction. In some cases it is possible to use a special message to indicate 'from now on there will be no more messages with a timestamp earlier than t', which consumers can use to trigger windows — but if several producers on different machines are generating events, each with their own minimum timestamp thresholds, the consumers need to keep track of each producer individually, and adding and removing producers is trickier in that case.

questions.question: A mobile app reports usage metrics but is used offline. What happens to its events?

options.text: It may continue to function while offline and buffer events locally on the device, sending them to a server when an internet connection is next available — which may be hours or even days later. To any consumers of that stream the events appear as extremely delayed stragglers
The events are lost while offline
The events are sent immediately regardless of connectivity
The events are discarded by the server as too old

questions.explanation: In this context the timestamp on the events should really be the time at which the user interaction occurred, according to the mobile device's local clock — but the clock on a user-controlled device often cannot be trusted, as it may be accidentally or deliberately set to the wrong time. The time at which the event was received by the server, according to the server's clock, is more likely to be accurate since the server is under your control, but less meaningful in terms of describing the user interaction.

questions.question: What three timestamps does the chapter say to log, and how do they correct a wrong device clock?

options.text: The time at which the event occurred according to the device clock; the time at which the event was sent to the server according to the device clock; and the time at which the event was received by the server according to the server clock. By subtracting the second timestamp from the third you can estimate the offset between the device clock and the server clock, assuming the network delay is negligible compared to the required timestamp accuracy. You can then apply that offset to the event timestamp, and thus estimate the true time at which the event actually occurred — assuming the device clock offset did not change between the time the event occurred and the time it was sent to the server
Only the device and server timestamps; no correction is possible
Only the server timestamp, which needs no correction
Four timestamps including the broker's

questions.explanation: This problem is not unique to stream processing — batch processing suffers from exactly the same issues of reasoning about time. It is just more noticeable in a streaming context, where we are more aware of the passage of time.

questions.question: Define a tumbling window, with the chapter's example.

options.text: A tumbling window has a fixed length, and every event belongs to exactly one window — for example if you have a 1-minute tumbling window, all the events with timestamps between 10:03:00 and 10:03:59 are grouped into one window, events between 10:04:00 and 10:04:59 into the next window, and so on. You could implement it by taking each event timestamp and rounding it down to the nearest minute to determine the window that it belongs to
A tumbling window overlaps with its neighbours
A tumbling window has no fixed length
A tumbling window groups events within an interval of each other

questions.explanation: Fixed length, exactly one window per event.

questions.question: Define a hopping window, with the chapter's example.

options.text: A hopping window also has a fixed length, but allows windows to overlap in order to provide some smoothing — for example a 5-minute window with a hop size of 1 minute would contain the events between 10:03:00 and 10:07:59, then the next window would cover events between 10:04:00 and 10:08:59, and so on. You can implement this by first calculating 1-minute tumbling windows and then aggregating over several adjacent windows
A hopping window has no fixed length and groups by inactivity
A hopping window never overlaps
A hopping window is per-user

questions.explanation: Fixed length with overlap, built from smaller tumbling windows.

questions.question: Define a sliding window, and why fixed-boundary windows would not group its example events.

options.text: A sliding window contains all the events that occur within some interval of each other — for example a 5-minute sliding window would cover events at 10:03:39 and 10:08:12, because they are less than 5 minutes apart. Note that tumbling and hopping 5-minute windows would not have put these two events in the same window, as they use fixed boundaries. A sliding window can be implemented by keeping a buffer of events sorted by time and removing old events when they expire from the window
A sliding window has fixed boundaries like a tumbling window
A sliding window is terminated by user inactivity
A sliding window has no length parameter

questions.explanation: No fixed boundaries — relative rather than absolute grouping. Readers most reliably confuse hopping with sliding: hopping windows still have fixed boundaries, whereas sliding windows have none at all and group events that are within the interval of each other.

questions.question: Define a session window and what makes it structurally unlike the others.

options.text: Unlike the other window types, a session window has no fixed duration: instead it is defined by grouping together all events for the same user that occur closely together in time, and the window ends when the user has been inactive for some time — for example if there have been no events for 30 minutes. Sessionization is a common requirement for website analytics
It has a fixed duration but overlaps with itself
It groups all users together rather than per-user
It is identical to a sliding window

questions.explanation: No fixed duration, per-user, terminated by an inactivity gap.

questions.question: Why are stream joins harder than batch joins, and what three types are there?

options.text: Since stream processing generalizes data pipelines to incremental processing of unbounded datasets, there is exactly the same need for joins on streams — but the fact that new events can appear anytime on a stream makes joins on streams more challenging than in batch jobs. The three types are stream-stream joins, stream-table joins and table-table joins
Because streams are sorted; the types are inner, outer and cross
Because streams are bounded; the types are hash, merge and nested loop
Joins are not possible on streams

questions.explanation: Unbounded arrival, three join shapes.

questions.question: Set up the stream-stream join example.

options.text: Say you have a search feature on your website and want to detect recent trends in searched-for URLs: every time someone types a search query you log an event containing the query and the results returned, and every time someone clicks one of the search results you log another event recording the click. To calculate the click-through rate for each URL in the search results, you need to bring together the events for the search action and the click action, which are connected by having the same session ID. Similar analyses are needed in advertising systems
Joining a click stream with a user profile database
Joining two database changelogs
Joining a stream with itself by timestamp

questions.explanation: Both inputs are activity events, joined on session ID.

questions.question: What can go wrong with the timing between search and click? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The click may never come if the user abandons their search

Even if it comes, the time between the search and the click may be highly variable — in many cases it might be a few seconds, but it could be as long as days or weeks, if the user leaves a browser tab open and comes back later
Due to variable network delays, the click event may even arrive before the search event
The chapter suggests joining a click with a search if they occur at most one hour apart

questions.explanation: Note that embedding the details of the search in the click event is not equivalent to joining the events: doing so would only tell you about the cases where the user clicked a search result, not about the searches where the user did not click any of the results — and to measure search quality you need accurate click-through rates, for which you need both the search events and the click events.

questions.question: Describe the state and algorithm for the stream-stream join.

options.text: To implement this type of join, a stream processor needs to maintain state — for example all the events that occurred in the last hour, indexed by session ID. Whenever a search event or click event occurs, it is added to the appropriate index, and the processor also checks the other index to see if another event for the same session ID has already arrived. If there is a matching event you emit an event saying which search result was clicked; if the search event expires without you seeing a matching click event, you emit an event saying which search results were not clicked
The processor queries a database per event and emits matches only
The processor buffers the entire stream history
The processor emits nothing when there is no match

questions.explanation: Two windowed indexes, with expiry emitting the negative case.

questions.question: Describe the stream-table join, and what the process is called.

options.text: It reuses the batch example of analyzing user activity events by joining a set of user activity events with a database of user profiles. It is natural to think of the user activity events as a stream, and to perform the same join on a continuous basis in a stream processor: the input is a stream of activity events containing a user ID, and the output is a stream of activity events in which the user ID has been augmented with profile information about the user. This process is sometimes known as enriching the activity events with information from the database
It joins two activity event streams within a window
It joins two database changelogs
It joins a stream with itself

questions.explanation: Activity events enriched from a database.

questions.question: How should the per-event database lookup be done?

options.text: One option would be querying a remote database for every event — but as discussed in the batch chapter, such remote queries are likely to be slow and risk overloading the database. Another approach is to load a copy of the database into the stream processor so that it can be queried locally without a network round-trip, a technique very similar to the hash joins of batch processing: the local copy of the database might be an in-memory hash table if it is small enough, or an index on the local disk
Only remote queries are possible for streams
The database must be rewritten as a stream
The lookup must be done in a separate batch job

questions.explanation: The difference from a batch job is that a batch process uses a point-in-time snapshot of the database as input, whereas a stream processor is long-running and the contents of the database are likely to change over time — so the local copy of the database needs to be kept up to date, which can be solved by change data capture: the stream processor subscribes to a changelog of the user profile database as well as the stream of activity events, and when a profile is created or modified it updates its local copy. Thus we obtain a join between two streams: the activity events and the profile updates.

questions.question: How does a stream-table join differ from a stream-stream join in its windows?

options.text: A stream-table join is very similar to a stream-stream join — the biggest difference is that for the table changelog stream the join uses a window that reaches back to the 'beginning of time', a conceptually infinite window, with newer versions of records overwriting older ones. For the stream input the join might not maintain a window at all
Both sides use a finite window of equal size
The stream side uses an infinite window and the table side a finite one
Neither side maintains a window

questions.explanation: Infinite window on the changelog, none on the activity stream.

questions.question: Which events must be processed to maintain Twitter's timeline cache? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: When user u sends a new tweet, it is added to the timeline of every user who is following u
When a user deletes a tweet, it is removed from all users' timelines
When user u1 starts following user u2, recent tweets by u2 are added to u1's timeline
When user u1 unfollows user u2, tweets by u2 are removed from u1's timeline

questions.explanation: When a user wants to view their home timeline it is too expensive to iterate over all the people the user is following, find their recent tweets and merge them — so instead there is a timeline cache, a kind of per-user 'inbox' to which tweets are written as they are sent, so that reading the timeline is a single lookup. To implement this cache maintenance in a stream processor you need streams of events for tweets (sending and deleting) and for follow relationships (following and unfollowing), and the process needs to maintain a database containing the set of followers for each user so it knows which timelines need to be updated when a new tweet arrives.

questions.question: What is the timeline process really maintaining?

options.text: A materialized view for a query that joins two tables — tweets and follows — where the join of the streams corresponds directly to the join of the tables in that query. The timelines are effectively a cache of the result of this query, updated every time the underlying tables change
A search index over tweets
An aggregation over a sliding window
A CEP pattern match

questions.explanation: A footnote gives the calculus reading: if you think of a stream as the derivative of a table and a join as a product of two tables u times v, then the stream of changes to the materialized join follows the product rule — the derivative of u times v equals u-prime v plus u v-prime — meaning any change of tweets is joined with the current followers, and any change of followers is joined with the current tweets.

questions.question: What do all three joins have in common, and why does ordering matter?

options.text: All three require the stream processor to maintain some state based on one join input, and query that state on messages from the other join input. The order of the events that maintain the state is important — it matters whether you first follow and then unfollow, or the other way round. In a partitioned log the ordering of events within a single partition is preserved, but there is typically no ordering guarantee across different streams or partitions
None require state; ordering is irrelevant
All require global ordering, which the log provides
Only the table-table join requires state

questions.explanation: This raises a question: if a user updates their profile, which activity events are joined with the old profile — processed before the profile update — and which are joined with the new profile, processed after? In general form: if state changes over time and you join with some state, what point in time do you use for the join? Another example: if you sell things you need to apply the right tax rate to invoices, which depends on the country or state, the type of product and the date of sale — so when joining sales to a table of tax rates, you probably want to join with the tax rate at the time of the sale, which may be different from the current tax rate if you are reprocessing historical data.

questions.question: What exactly goes wrong when cross-stream ordering is undetermined?

options.text: The join becomes nondeterministic: you cannot rerun the same job on the same input and necessarily get the same result, because the events on the input streams may be interleaved in a different way when you run the job again
The join fails with an error
The join loses events
The join duplicates events

questions.explanation: In data warehouses this issue is known as a slowly changing dimension (SCD), and it is often addressed by using a unique identifier for a particular version of the joined record: for example every time the tax rate changes it is given a new identifier, and the invoice includes the identifier for the tax rate at the time of sale. That makes the join deterministic, but has the consequence that log compaction is not possible, since all versions of the records in the table need to be retained.

questions.question: Match each join description to its type.

options.text: Both inputs being database changelogs, with every change on one side joined with the latest state of the other and the result being a stream of changes to the materialized view, is a table-table join. Both inputs being activity events, with the operator searching for related events that occur within some window of time — possibly matching two actions taken by the same user within 30 minutes of each other, and possibly with both inputs being the same stream in a self-join — is a stream-stream join. One input being activity events and the other a database changelog, with the operator keeping a local copy of the database up to date and querying it to output an enriched activity event, is a stream-table join
The changelog pair is a stream-stream join and the activity pair is a table-table join
All three descriptions are stream-table joins
The enrichment case is a table-table join

questions.explanation: Both changelogs is table-table, both activity streams is stream-stream, one of each is stream-table.

questions.question: Why is batch fault tolerance easy, and what does it guarantee?

options.text: If a task in a MapReduce job fails it can simply be started again on another machine, and the output of the failed task is discarded. This transparent retry is possible because input files are immutable, each task writes its output to a separate file on HDFS, and output is only made visible when a task completes successfully. So the batch approach to fault tolerance ensures that the output of the batch job is the same as if nothing had gone wrong, even if in fact some tasks did fail
Batch jobs never fail, so no mechanism is needed
Batch jobs checkpoint continuously like stream jobs
Batch jobs use transactions on HDFS

questions.explanation: It appears as though every input record was processed exactly once — no records are skipped and none are processed twice. Although restarting tasks means that records may in fact be processed multiple times, the visible effect in the output is as if they had only been processed once: this principle is known as exactly-once semantics, although effectively-once would be a more descriptive term, since records genuinely are sometimes processed more than once and only the visible effect is once-only.

questions.question: Why doesn't the batch trick transfer to streams?

options.text: Because waiting until a task is finished before making its output visible is not an option: a stream is infinite, so you can never finish processing it
Because streams have no output
Because streams are immutable
Because streams are already fault-tolerant

questions.explanation: No completion point means no atomic reveal point.

questions.question: Describe microbatching, its typical batch size, and the compromise that sets it.

options.text: One solution is to break the stream into small blocks and treat each block like a miniature batch process — an approach called microbatching, used in Spark Streaming. The batch size is typically around one second, which is the result of a performance compromise: smaller batches incur greater scheduling and coordination overhead, while larger batches mean a longer delay before results of the stream processor become visible
Microbatching uses batches of one minute, set by network latency
Microbatching uses batches of one millisecond, set by CPU speed
Microbatching has no configurable batch size

questions.explanation: Microbatching also implicitly provides a tumbling window equal to the batch size, based on processing time rather than event timestamps — so any jobs that require larger windows need to explicitly carry over state from one microbatch to the next.

questions.question: Describe Flink's rolling checkpoints.

options.text: A variant approach, used in Apache Flink, is to periodically generate rolling checkpoints of state and write them to durable storage. If a stream operator crashes it can restart from its most recent checkpoint and discard any output generated between the last checkpoint and the crash. The checkpoints are triggered by barriers in the message stream, similar to the boundaries between microbatches, but without forcing a particular window size
Flink uses microbatching with a fixed one-second window
Flink replicates all state synchronously to three nodes
Flink has no fault tolerance mechanism

questions.explanation: Barriers without a forced window size is the advantage over microbatching.

questions.question: Both approaches give exactly-once semantics only within the framework. What breaks that?

options.text: As soon as output leaves the stream processor — for example by writing to a database, sending messages to an external message broker, or sending emails — the framework is no longer able to discard the output of a failed batch. In that case, restarting a failed task causes the external side effect to happen twice, and microbatching or checkpointing alone is not sufficient to prevent this problem
Nothing breaks it; the guarantee extends to all outputs
Only database writes break it; messaging is safe
Only emails break it; databases are safe

questions.explanation: Any externally visible side effect escapes the framework's ability to discard.

questions.question: What must commit atomically for exactly-once processing to appear? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: All outputs and side effects of processing an event take effect if and only if the processing is successful — including any messages sent to downstream operators or external messaging systems, such as email or push notifications
Any database writes
Any changes to operator state

Any acknowledgment of input messages, including moving the consumer offset forward in a log-based message broker. Those things either all need to happen atomically, or none of them must happen, but they should not go out of sync with each other

questions.explanation: In more restricted environments it is possible to implement such an atomic commit facility efficiently: this approach is used in Google Cloud Dataflow and VoltDB, and there are plans to add similar features to Apache Kafka. Unlike XA, these implementations do not attempt to provide transactions across heterogeneous technologies, but instead keep them internal by managing both state changes and messaging within the stream processing framework — and the transaction protocol's overhead can be amortized by processing several input messages within a single transaction.

questions.question: Define an idempotent operation with the chapter's positive and negative examples.

options.text: An idempotent operation is one that you can perform multiple times, and it has the same effect as if you performed it only once. For example setting a key in a key-value store to some fixed value is idempotent, since writing the value again simply overwrites the value with an identical value, whereas incrementing a counter is not idempotent, since performing the increment again means the value is incremented twice
An idempotent operation can only be performed once; incrementing qualifies
Both setting and incrementing are idempotent
Neither setting nor incrementing is idempotent

questions.explanation: We want to discard the partial output of any failed tasks so that they can be safely retried without taking effect twice. Distributed transactions are one way of achieving that goal; another way is to rely on idempotence.

questions.question: How can a non-idempotent write be made idempotent?

options.text: With a bit of extra metadata. For example when consuming messages from Kafka, every message has a persistent, monotonically increasing offset — so when writing a value to an external database you can include the offset of the message that triggered the last write with the value. Thus you can tell whether an update has already been applied, and avoid performing the same update again. The state handling in Storm's Trident is based on a similar idea
By wrapping it in a distributed transaction, which is the only option
By retrying it until it succeeds
It cannot be made idempotent

questions.explanation: An offset stamped alongside the value lets the write detect its own replay.

questions.question: What assumptions does idempotence rest on? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: That restarting a failed task must replay the same messages in the same order — a log-based message broker does this
That the processing must be deterministic

That no other node may concurrently update the same value. When failing over from one processing node to another, fencing may be required to prevent interference from a node that is thought to be dead but is actually alive
That the database must support two-phase commit

questions.explanation: Despite all those caveats, idempotent operations can be an effective way of achieving exactly-once semantics with only a small overhead.

questions.question: What kinds of state must survive a failure, and where can it be held?

options.text: Any stream process that requires state — for example windowed aggregations such as counters, averages and histograms, and tables and indexes used for joins — must ensure that state can be recovered after a failure. One option is to keep the state in a remote datastore and replicate it, although having to query a remote database for each individual message can be slow. An alternative is to keep state local to the stream processor and replicate it periodically, so that when the stream processor is recovering from a failure the new task can read the replicated state and resume processing without data loss
Only counters need recovery, and only remote state works
No state needs recovery in stream processing
Only local state works; remote state is impossible

questions.explanation: Local plus periodic replication, or remote with per-message latency.

questions.question: Match the three frameworks to their state-replication mechanisms.

options.text: Flink periodically captures snapshots of operator state and writes them to durable storage such as HDFS; Samza and Kafka Streams replicate state changes by sending them to a dedicated Kafka topic with log compaction, similar to change data capture; and VoltDB replicates state by redundantly processing each input message on several nodes
Flink uses Kafka topics; Samza uses HDFS snapshots; VoltDB uses remote storage
All three use HDFS snapshots
All three use redundant processing

questions.explanation: Snapshots, compacted changelog topics, and redundant processing respectively.

questions.question: When is it unnecessary to replicate state at all?

options.text: In some cases it may not even be necessary to replicate the state, because it can be rebuilt from the input streams: for example if the state consists of aggregations over a fairly short window, it may be fast enough to simply replay the input events corresponding to that window; and if the state is a local replica of a database maintained by change data capture, the database can also be rebuilt from the log-compacted change stream
Never; state must always be replicated
Only when the state is empty
Only when the job is read-only

questions.explanation: However, all of these trade-offs depend on the performance characteristics of the underlying infrastructure: in some systems network delay may be lower than disk access latency, and network bandwidth may be comparable to disk bandwidth. There is no universally ideal trade-off for all situations, and the merits of local versus remote state may also shift as storage and networking technologies evolve.

questions.question: How does the Summary relate stream processing to Chapter 10?

options.text: In many ways stream processing is very much like the batch processing of Chapter 10, but done continuously on unbounded, never-ending streams rather than on a fixed-size input — and from this perspective, message brokers and event logs serve as the streaming equivalent of a filesystem
Stream processing is fundamentally unrelated to batch processing
Stream processing replaces filesystems with databases
Stream processing is batch processing with smaller inputs

questions.explanation: Brokers and logs as the streaming filesystem.

questions.question: Give the Summary's definition of the AMQP/JMS-style broker and its appropriate workload.

options.text: The broker assigns individual messages to consumers, and consumers acknowledge individual messages when they have been successfully processed; messages are deleted from the broker once they have been acknowledged. This approach is appropriate as an asynchronous form of RPC, for example in a task queue, where the exact order of message processing is not important and there is no need to go back and read old messages again after they have been processed
The broker assigns whole partitions; appropriate for ordered high-throughput streams
The broker retains all messages; appropriate for derived data systems
The broker drops messages; appropriate for metrics

questions.explanation: Per-message assignment and deletion on acknowledgment, for task queues.

questions.question: Give the Summary's definition of the log-based broker and what it resembles.

options.text: The broker assigns all messages in a partition to the same consumer node, and always delivers messages in the same order. Parallelism is achieved through partitioning, and consumers track their progress by checkpointing the offset of the last message they have processed. The broker retains messages on disk, so it is possible to jump back and reread old messages if necessary. This approach resembles the replication logs found in databases and log-structured storage engines, and is especially appropriate for stream processing systems that consume input streams and generate derived state or derived output streams
It assigns individual messages and deletes them on acknowledgment
It resembles a relational table
It resembles a task queue

questions.explanation: Partition assignment, offset checkpointing, and disk retention.

questions.question: Where do streams come from, and what does log compaction add?

options.text: Streams come from user activity events, sensors providing periodic readings, and data feeds such as market data in finance. It is also useful to think of the writes to a database as a stream: we can capture the changelog — the history of all changes made to a database — either implicitly through change data capture or explicitly through event sourcing. Log compaction allows the stream to retain a full copy of the contents of a database
Only from message brokers; compaction reduces retention
Only from databases; compaction removes all history
Only from sensors; compaction is unrelated

questions.explanation: Representing databases as streams opens up powerful opportunities for integrating systems: you can keep derived data systems such as search indexes, caches and analytics systems continually up to date by consuming the log of changes and applying them to the derived system, and you can even build fresh views onto existing data by starting from scratch and consuming the log of changes from the beginning all the way to the present.

questions.question: Which purposes of stream processing does the Summary list, and which time difficulties does it recall?

options.text: Searching for event patterns (complex event processing), computing windowed aggregations (stream analytics), and keeping derived data systems up to date (materialized views). The time difficulties: the distinction between processing time and event timestamps, and the problem of dealing with straggler events that arrive after you thought your window was complete
Only analytics and materialized views; the difficulty is clock skew alone
Only pattern matching; the difficulty is ordering alone
Only materialized views; there are no time difficulties

questions.explanation: Three purposes and two time problems.

questions.question: Restate the Summary's fault-tolerance argument and its four mechanisms.

options.text: As with batch processing we need to discard the partial output of any failed tasks — but since a stream process is long-running and produces output continuously, we can't simply discard all output. Instead a finer-grained recovery mechanism can be used, based on microbatching, checkpointing, transactions, or idempotent writes
Stream jobs discard all output on failure, as batch jobs do
Stream jobs cannot recover from failure
Stream jobs rely solely on replication

questions.explanation: Finer-grained recovery, via four mechanisms.
